title: Reform close
hookLine: schools, presses, peaceful protest and a code: the panth renewed itself

cards: An old house, handed down. The roof leaks, the wiring is strange, someone has painted over the carvings by the door. You could leave.
You could tear it down. Or you could do the slow thing: scrape the paint back, fix the roof, find the original drawings and learn how it was meant to be.
Through this whole block, that's how the reformers described their own work. Not building a new house. Restoring the one the Gurus left.

teach.b: The block opened with voices calling back: Baba Dayal turning people to the formless One, and Baba Ram Singh and the Namdharis, simple and firm, remembered at Malerkotla and in exile in Burma.

Then schools and presses: the Singh Sabhas in Amritsar and Lahore, Giani Ditt Singh and Professor Gurmukh Singh, Khalsa College, Mahan Kosh, Macauliffe's volumes, Bhai Vir Singh and his heroine Sundri, suniai, the Chief Khalsa Diwan, Anand Karaj, and the presses that spread it all.
Sikhs learned to explain their faith in print, in Punjabi and in English.
Then peaceful protest: kandh, the outrage over siropa, the SGPC, Tarn Taran and Nankana, the keys, Guru ka Bagh, Panja Sahib and Jaito, until the Gurdwara Act gave the shrines back to the sangat.
Beside them stood the Ghadar workers far from home, and men like Udham Singh and Bhagat Singh, whose paths Sikhs still weigh.
Then the code and the people: Master Tara Singh, the Rehat Maryada, the Jail Letters, Sant Attar Singh's schools, and the women who taught, wrote and marched.

Underneath it all is a line from the Japji, at Ang 4 of the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Nanak says that when hands and feet are muddy, water washes them clean, and when the mind is stained, it's washed by love of the Name.
Washing isn't a one-time thing. You do it again.

how: Sikhs remember the Singh Sabha and gurdwara reform movements through their institutions still standing: schools and colleges, Sikh presses and libraries, the SGPC and the Rehat Maryada, and the gurdwaras where the sakas of those years are told.

o: a council that governs Sikh shrines and schools
reform or improvement, renewing what was handed down
a new beginning that replaces the old entirely

games.q: the block, looking back — tap the pairs.
p: the mind washed by the Name

s: the reformers said they were building a new religion
they described their work as returning to and explaining what the Gurus left: schools, presses, protest and a code.
the gurdwara campaigns ended with a law
the Gurdwara Act placed historic gurdwaras under an elected Sikh body.
in the Japji, washing the mind is done once
the image is of hands and feet washed whenever they're muddy; renewal is repeated.

games.q: the house the Gurus left has leaks and painted-over carvings. what does the panth of these years do?
o: tear it down and build something new.
restore it, slowly, room by room.
games.why: through schools, presses, peaceful protest and a shared code, the reformers worked to restore what the Gurus left.

practice: Bring to mind one practice in your life that used to be clear and has grown cloudy: a prayer you used to say, a walk you used to take, a way you used to speak to someone.
Without scolding yourself, look at it the way you'd look at a smudged window, and on each breath out picture wiping the glass clean. If you pray, say Waheguru as you breathe out.

wordCard.voice: Sudhar, reform or improvement: the gurdwara reform movement is called the Gurdwara Sudhar Lehar. Schools, presses, peaceful protest and a shared code helped the panth renew itself. Today's word.

orig.note: sudhar, reform or improvement; the gurdwara reform movement is called the Gurdwara Sudhar Lehar.

carryVoice: Your line: renew. Tomorrow the story leaves Punjab again, for the trenches. That's the block.
